title: In our own words
goals: Use C2 phrasal verbs accurately (separable, inseparable and three-part verbs) and choose the appropriate register.
Use idioms about language and communication without translating them literally from Spanish.
Adjust your register (informal, neutral, formal) to your interlocutor and medium, using courteous indirectness.
Handle euphemism, dysphemism and connotation, and recognise doublespeak.
Speak with nuance about identity, culture, accents and dialects (code-switching, heritage speaker, accentism).
Consciously adapt your register to each context, in speech and in writing.

learn.title: C2 phrasal verbs: syntax, nuance and register
learn.html:
At C2 the problem is no longer knowing that they exist, but where to place the object, what nuance they add and which register they belong to. Almost all the phrasal verbs at this level are idiomatic: the meaning cannot be worked out from the parts (come across as has nothing to do with "coming" or "crossing").

TypeObject ruleExample
IntransitiveNo objectThe effect soon wore off. / Many dialects are dying out.
Transitive separableThe object goes between the verb and the particle, or after it; a pronoun always goes in the middleShe spelled out the terms. / She spelled the terms out. / She spelled them out.
Transitive inseparableThe object always goes after the particleI came across the word by chance. / He takes after his father.
Three-part (verb + adverb + preposition)Inseparable: the object goes at the endI can't put up with it. / She lives up to her reputation.
  • Long object: with separable verbs, a very long object usually goes after the particle so the sentence does not "break": She spelled out in no uncertain terms exactly what she expected.
  • Passive: the particle stays attached to the verb: She was looked down on by her classmates. (the final preposition is not dropped).
  • Preposition at the end: in neutral or informal register this is natural: the dialect I grew up with. In very formal register the dialect with which I grew up is preferred.
  • Register: most phrasal verbs sound neutral or informal, and their Latinate equivalents (postpone, tolerate, convey) sound more formal; but some are perfectly formal (carry out, point out, set out). You have to hear them in context, not just memorise them.
  • Polysemy: the same phrasal verb can have a literal and a figurative sense: pick up (to collect / to acquire an accent without trying / to understand); come across (to encounter / to give the impression of: She comes across as aloof).
  • Nuance of effortlessness: pick up a language means acquiring it through exposure; learn suggests study; brush up on means refreshing something you already knew.

watch.wrong: She picked up it from her grandmother.
watch.right: She picked it up from her grandmother.
watch.why: With a separable verb, the object pronoun always goes between the verb and the particle.

watch.wrong: I can't put it up with.
watch.right: I can't put up with it.
watch.why: Three-part verbs are inseparable: the object goes at the end.

watch.wrong: She was looked down by her classmates.
watch.right: She was looked down on by her classmates.
watch.why: In the passive the preposition is kept: look down on → be looked down on.

watch.wrong: He spelled out me the rules.
watch.right: He spelled the rules out to me.
watch.why: After the particle an indirect object cannot follow without "to"; restructure with "to" or place the direct object first.

learn.title: Idioms about language and communication: how they behave
learn.html:
An idiom is a semi-fixed unit: its overall meaning does not derive from its words. Spanish speakers typically make two mistakes: calquing the Spanish idiom word for word (andarse por las ramas ≠ walk around the branches), and altering a part that does not allow change.

IdiomApproximate Spanish equivalentRoom for variation
beat around the bushandarse por las ramasIt conjugates: He kept beating around the bush.
hit the nail on the headdar en el clavoPast tense: You've hit the nail on the head.
get the wrong end of the stickentender al revés / malinterpretarAccepts get hold of the wrong end of the stick.
call a spade a spadellamar al pan, pan y al vino, vinoAlmost unalterable; it connotes frankness, sometimes bluntly so.
bite your tonguemorderse la lenguaThe possessive agrees with the subject: I bit my tongue.
  • Grammatical agreement yes, lexical change no: tense, number and possessive are adjusted (She bit her tongue), but no word is substituted (hit the nail in the head is an error).
  • Fixed articles and prepositions: in a nutshell (not in nutshell), at cross purposes (not in).
  • Rhetorical effect: a well-placed idiom sounds natural; three in a row sound like a catalogue. In academic writing they are used sparingly, and sometimes in quotation marks or with a wink: to borrow a phrase, ...
  • Creative twist (native level): speakers play with idioms: Beating around the bush? You're practically mowing it. It is only funny if the listener recognises the original.
  • Difference between idiom and collocation: make a point is a collocation (a habitual combination), whereas get the wrong end of the stick is an idiom (figurative meaning, not literal).

watch.why: Calque of "andarse por las ramas": English uses bush, not branches.

watch.wrong: You hit the nail in the head.
watch.right: You hit the nail on the head.
watch.why: The preposition is fixed: on the head.

watch.wrong: I think we have the cables crossed.
watch.right: I think we've got our wires crossed.
watch.why: Calque of "cables cruzados": in English they are wires, and the idiom is get / have our wires crossed.
The article "a" is part of the idiom.

learn.title: Register: from colloquial to formal (and how to choose)
learn.html:
English has no grammatical equivalent of tú/usted: formality is built with vocabulary, syntax and degree of indirectness. A Spanish speaker, used to usted doing the work, often sounds too blunt in English (I want…) or, when overcorrecting, absurdly stiff.

ColloquialNeutralFormal / written
find outdiscoverascertain
put offdelaypostpone, defer
look intoinvestigateexamine, scrutinise
get rid ofremovedispose of, eliminate
a lot ofplenty ofa considerable amount of
Any chance you could…?Could you…?I should be grateful if you could…
Sorry about that.I'm sorry.Please accept my apologies.
  • Grammar and register: contractions and ellipsis (Seen the film?, Can't wait.) are colloquial; passives, nominalisations and long subordinate clauses are formal; preposition + which/whom is formal (the committee of which I am a member); a preposition at the end is neutral (the committee I'm a member of).
  • Indirectness = courtesy: I wonder if you could… is more polite than Could you…?, and that is more polite than Can you…?. Avoid I want with strangers: I'd like… / I was hoping to….
  • Colloquial markers: well, you know, I mean, sort of, or something, mate. Remove them from formal texts; use them in moderation in informal ones so you do not sound stiff.
  • Factors that decide register: power relationship, social distance, medium (email, message, speech) and purpose. Adjusting register to each interlocutor is a form of code-switching, not of insincerity.
  • Do not mix: a formal greeting with a colloquial body (Dear Dr Hale, gonna need that by Friday), or a pompous passive with a friend, sounds sarcastic.

watch.wrong: Dear Ms Okafor, I'm gonna need the figures by Friday.
watch.right: Dear Ms Okafor, I will need the figures by Friday.
watch.why: Mixed register: a formal greeting requires a formal body (no "gonna").

watch.wrong: I want to speak with the manager.
watch.right: I'd like to speak to the manager.
watch.why: "I want" sounds abrupt to a stranger; "I'd like" softens it without losing firmness.

watch.wrong: I have been informed by my friend that the party is cancelled, mate.
watch.why: A formal passive with a friend sounds distant or sarcastic: keep it colloquial with "mate".

learn.title: Euphemism, dysphemism and connotation
learn.html:
Two words with the same denotation (referent) can carry opposite connotations. Choosing one or the other is taking a position. Euphemism softens what is uncomfortable; dysphemism deliberately hardens it; doublespeak uses euphemisms to conceal something.

DirectEuphemismNuance note
diepass away / pass onCondolences and respectful treatment; kick the bucket is a humorous dysphemism.
fire (staff)let go / make redundant / downsizeCorporate; rightsizing and restructuring can sound like doublespeak.
unemployedbetween jobsSelf-protection: it suggests something temporary.
old peopleolder people / senior citizensRespectful; the elderly sounds clinical and distant.
poor countrydeveloping countryShifts the perspective from "lack" to "process".
toiletrestroom / bathroom / the looThe taboo shifts: the euphemistic "treadmill" effect.
  • Connotation scale: thrifty / frugal (positive), economical (neutral), cheap / stingy (negative); determined (+), stubborn (−), pig-headed (−−). The word you choose reveals your judgement.
  • "Euphemism treadmill": a euphemism picks up the taboo of what it replaces and, over time, becomes offensive; it then has to be replaced (handicapped → disabled → person with a disability). This is why some labels, such as handicapped, now sound old-fashioned.
  • When to soften: condolences, bad news, health, age, disability. When not to: safety instructions, contracts, precise diagnoses: there, vagueness is dangerous.
  • Beware of affection: adjectives that can be affectionate in Spanish (gordito, flaquito) have no warm equivalent in English; fat or skinny usually sound like an insult.
  • Doublespeak: collateral damage, enhanced interrogation, pre-owned: language that hides or disguises. Spotting it is part of reading between the lines.

watch.wrong: My neighbour, who is handicapped, volunteers at the library.
watch.right: My neighbour, who has a disability, volunteers at the library.
watch.why: "Handicapped" sounds outdated; today "person with a disability" or "disabled person" is preferred.

watch.wrong: I'm so sorry your father is dead.
watch.right: I'm so sorry for your loss.
watch.why: In condolences, "dead" is blunt; people say "for your loss" or "passed away".

watch.wrong: He is very cheap, and I admire that.
watch.right: He is very frugal, and I admire that.
watch.why: "Cheap" applied to a person is pejorative; if you admire the trait, use "frugal" or "thrifty".

learn.title: Useful phrases: adjusting register and reformulating
learn.html:
• Formal: I am writing with regard to… / I should be grateful if you could… / Might I suggest…? / Please do not hesitate to contact me.
  • Neutral: Could you possibly…? / Just checking whether… / I was wondering if…
  • Informal: Any chance you could…? / Mind if I…? / Sorry, I didn't catch that.
  • Reformulating without belittling the other person: What I mean is… / Put another way,… / To put it more simply,…
  • Softening an uncomfortable truth: Not to put too fine a point on it,… / With the greatest respect,… / I don't mean to be rude, but…
  • Deliberate vagueness (colloquial): sort of, kind of, or something, and stuff: they soften, but overusing them undermines authority in formal contexts.
  • Talking about your own language: I sound different depending on who I'm talking to. / I tend to slip into Spanish when I'm tired. / It doesn't quite translate.

practice.title: Phrasal verbs: the right particle
practice.instructions: Write the missing particle to complete the phrasal verb.

items.prompt: Her grandmother's rolling accent has rubbed ___ on all her grandchildren.
answers: off
items.explain: rub off on = to influence someone by example, passing on a quality or habit.

items.prompt: Please don't talk ___ to me as though I were a child.
answers: down
items.explain: talk down to = to speak to someone condescendingly, as if they were less intelligent.

items.prompt: I can't put up ___ people who correct my grammar at dinner.
answers: with
items.explain: put up with = tolerate; a three-part verb (verb + particle + preposition).

items.prompt: She's rusty, so she's brushing ___ on her German before the move.
answers: up
items.explain: brush up on = to refresh one's knowledge of something.

items.prompt: When the funding ended, the museum had to fall ___ on volunteers.
answers: back
items.explain: fall back on = to resort to something when other options fail.

items.prompt: Many of the region's minority languages have died ___ within two generations.
answers: out
items.explain: die out = to become extinct, to gradually disappear.

items.prompt: He didn't say it directly, so I asked him to spell it ___.
answers: out
items.explain: spell out = to explain in full detail; with a pronoun, the pronoun goes in the middle.

practice.title: Phrasal verbs: meaning and object placement
practice.instructions: Choose the correct option or correct the sentence.

items.prompt: Mariana always ___ her achievements, which makes her seem modest.
items.explain: play down = to minimise, to make something seem less important.

items.prompt: My manager ___ as rather cold at first, but she's actually very warm.
items.explain: come across as = to give the impression of being.

items.prompt: She picked up it from her grandmother.
answers: She picked it up from her grandmother.
items.explain: The object pronoun goes between the verb and the particle.

items.prompt: Her classmates looked down her because of her accent.
answers: Her classmates looked down on her because of her accent.
Her classmates looked down upon her because of her accent.
items.explain: look down on is a three-part verb (verb + particle + preposition); the object goes after "on".

items.prompt: We spent two hours ___ the differences between the translations.
items.explain: iron out = to resolve or smooth out differences.

items.prompt: We couldn't get our point across them.
answers: We couldn't get our point across to them.
items.explain: get something across to someone: the preposition "to" is missing.

items.prompt: Whenever she phones her mother, she ___ the dialect of her childhood.
items.explain: slip into = to switch, without meaning to, into a different way of speaking.

items.prompt: You've hit the nail on the ___: that's exactly the problem.
answers: head
items.explain: hit the nail on the head = to be exactly right.

items.prompt: I think you got the wrong end of the ___; she never said she was leaving.
answers: stick
items.explain: get the wrong end of the stick = to misunderstand.

items.prompt: Something that is 'lost in translation' is:
options: a nuance that does not survive the move to another language
items.explain: lost in translation = a nuance that does not carry over from one language to another.

items.prompt: Let me put it in a ___: we need more time and fewer meetings.
answers: nutshell
items.explain: in a nutshell = in brief, summarised very concisely.

items.prompt: She has a way of words, and everyone listens.
answers: She has a way with words, and everyone listens.
items.explain: have a way with words: the preposition is "with".

items.prompt: We both thought we agreed, but we were clearly talking at ___.
items.explain: talk at cross purposes = to misunderstand each other because each is talking about something different.

items.prompt: He bit his language rather than argue at the funeral.
answers: He bit his tongue rather than argue at the funeral.
items.explain: bite one's tongue = to hold back a comment or remark.

practice.title: Register: formal, neutral and informal
practice.instructions: Choose the appropriate option or complete.

items.prompt: Which is the most formal way to ask a colleague to send a file?
options: Send me that file, will you?
Any chance you could send that over?
I should be grateful if you could forward the file.
items.explain: "I should be grateful if you could…" is the most formal formula.

items.prompt: Choose the everyday phrasal verb that matches the formal verb 'ascertain'.
items.explain: ascertain = find out, establish (formal).

items.prompt: Which sentence suits an email to a senior client you have never met?
options: I regret that I shall be unable to attend on Tuesday.
Tuesday's a no-go, I'm afraid, mate.
items.explain: Formal passive and "regret that" construction: appropriate register.

items.prompt: Which message sounds like a text to a close friend?
options: I shall be delighted to attend.
Can't make it tonight, sorry. Work's mental.
Kindly note that I shall be unavailable.
items.explain: Ellipsis, contraction and colloquial vocabulary.

items.prompt: We have decided to ___ the vote until March. (formal verb for 'put off')
answers: postpone
defer
items.explain: postpone / defer = formal equivalents of "put off".

items.prompt: The committee of ___ I am a member has approved the plan. (formal)
answers: which
items.explain: Formal register: preposition + which.

items.prompt: In English, the difference between formal and informal address is carried mainly by:
options: vocabulary, grammar and degree of indirectness
items.explain: English has no tú/usted distinction: formality is conveyed through vocabulary, syntax and indirectness.

practice.title: Euphemism, dysphemism and connotation
practice.instructions: Choose the option or correct the sentence.

items.prompt: Which is a euphemism for 'died'?
items.explain: pass away = a common euphemism for "died".

items.prompt: 'We're letting twenty staff go' is a euphemism for:
items.explain: let go = to dismiss staff, in a softened way.

items.prompt: She isn't stingy; she's just ___. (a positive word for 'careful with money')
answers: thrifty
frugal
items.explain: thrifty / frugal have positive connotations.

items.prompt: My neighbour, who is handicapped, volunteers at the library.
answers: My neighbour, who is disabled, volunteers at the library.
My neighbour, who has a disability, volunteers at the library.
items.explain: Handicapped sounds outdated and can be offensive.

items.prompt: Someone who won't change their mind: which word carries the most positive connotation?
items.explain: determined (+), stubborn (−), pig-headed (−−).

items.prompt: 'Collateral damage' used by a spokesperson for civilian deaths is an example of:
items.explain: A euphemism that hides the truth = doublespeak.

items.prompt: 'Between jobs' is a gentle way of saying that someone is ___.
answers: unemployed
out of work
jobless
items.explain: between jobs = unemployed, in a softened way.

items.prompt: She alternates between Spanish and English mid-sentence depending on who is listening. This is called code-___.
answers: switching
items.explain: code-switching = alternating between languages or registers.

items.prompt: English used between a Thai and a Brazilian businessperson is functioning as a ___.
items.explain: lingua franca = a shared language used for communication between speakers of different first languages.

items.prompt: A 'heritage speaker' is someone who:
options: grew up hearing a family language at home but mostly uses another outside it
studies dead languages at a museum
items.explain: heritage speaker = someone who grew up hearing a language at home (often a minority or immigrant language) but is more dominant in another.

items.prompt: A slow way of speaking with lengthened vowels, often linked to the American South, is a ___.
answers: drawl
items.explain: drawl = a slow way of speaking with stretched vowels.

items.prompt: Which word names the specialised vocabulary of a profession, often opaque to outsiders?
items.explain: jargon = the specialised vocabulary of a profession or group.

items.prompt: Judging someone's intelligence by how they speak is a form of linguistic ___. (prejudice / discrimination)
answers: discrimination
prejudice
items.explain: Accentism = linguistic discrimination/prejudice.

items.prompt: Two dialects are 'mutually intelligible' when:
options: speakers can understand each other without special study
both have the same number of speakers
items.explain: mutually intelligible = speakers of each can understand the other without prior study.

practice.title: Put the sentences in order
practice.instructions: Put the words in order to form a correct sentence.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form a sentence or question.
answers: She picked it up from her grandmother.
items.explain: The pronoun goes between the verb and the particle.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form a sentence or question.
answers: Not everything can be put into words.
items.explain: Passive with a modal: "can be put into words".

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form a sentence or question.
answers: I wonder if you could possibly give me a hand.
items.explain: Courteous indirectness: "I wonder if you could…"

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form a sentence or question.
answers: Her accent has rubbed off on all of us.
items.explain: rub off on = to influence someone by example.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form a sentence or question.
answers: He came across as far more confident than he felt.
items.explain: come across as + adjective.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form a sentence or question.

write.prompt: Reflective essay of 300 to 400 words: "Does speaking another language change who you are?" Use at least six phrasal verbs from the unit (e.g. pick up, rub off on, hold on to, slip into, tone down, come across as), two idioms about language, one well-justified euphemism and a note on your own register when speaking with your family, at work and with your friends.
checklist: Between 300 and 400 words with clear paragraphs and a thesis
At least 6 well-placed phrasal verbs (pronouns between verb and particle in separable ones)
2 idioms with their parts unaltered
One euphemism and a note on its connotation
Register contrast between two contexts (family / work / friends)
Identity vocabulary (heritage, code-switching, sense of belonging…)
A conclusion that returns to the thesis
write.model:
When I was a child, English was a school subject; now it is a second skin, or perhaps a second voice. The question is whether that voice has changed the person using it. I would argue that it has, though less dramatically than the romantic version suggests: a language does not replace the self, but it does draw out sides of it that might otherwise have stayed dormant.

I picked up most of my English late, through films, songs and years of stubborn practice, and some habits of the new language have rubbed off on me. In Spanish I am inclined to beat around the bush; in English I get to the point, and I am quicker to say "I disagree" without cushioning it. In Spanish I hold on to ceremony; in English I slip into a brisker, drier humour that my relatives find faintly alien. I have also learned to tone down my enthusiasm in certain settings, since what sounds warm at home can come across as excessive in an office. Some of my jokes, of course, are lost in translation.

That is where register matters. With my family I speak a relaxed, affectionate Spanish full of diminutives and in-jokes, and when I switch into English for a visiting cousin, we all feel the shift. At work I am measured and careful: I say "I am afraid there has been a slight delay" when I mean the project has collapsed. It is a euphemism that spares feelings while hardly concealing the truth, although its connotation of regret can also read as evasion. With friends, finally, I speak a hybrid that no dictionary records, shifting mid-sentence from one language to the other. Linguists call this code-switching, and I regard it less as a lapse than as a badge of belonging.

None of this means I have been replaced by someone else. My heritage remains the source of my accent, my jokes and my stubbornness. Learning another language taught me that every way of speaking is a way of seeing, and that I can have more than one without losing my own.

So yes, speaking another language changes who you are, but only by adding to it. My sense of self used to have one voice. It now has two, and I am no longer sure I could do without either.

write.prompt: Write a formal letter of 300 to 400 words to the editor of a newspaper about prejudice against accents at work, in a respectful but firm tone. At the end add a short message (2–3 sentences) to a friend telling them you sent it, in colloquial register.
checklist: Letter of 300 to 400 words with formal greeting and sign-off
Coherent formal vocabulary (ascertain, postpone, regarding…) with no contractions
At least one euphemism or term with a deliberately chosen connotation

Courteous indirectness formulas (I should be grateful if…)
Colloquial closing message with contractions and informal markers, clearly different in register
write.model:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing regarding your recent article on graduate recruitment, which, to my disappointment, made no mention of a form of prejudice that many employees experience daily: bias against regional and foreign accents.

I should be grateful if you would allow me to explain why this matters. Accentism, as it has come to be known, is the practice of judging a person's competence, intelligence or reliability by the way he or she sounds. Studies have repeatedly ascertained that listeners rate speakers of certain varieties as less capable, even when the content of what they say is identical. A candidate whose vernacular differs from that of the interviewer may therefore be passed over or, in the polite language of human resources, "not progressed to the next stage". Such a phrase may sound neutral, but its connotation is anything but.

It is worth recalling that accents are not deficiencies. Most varieties of English are mutually intelligible, and clarity depends far more on the listener's willingness to listen than on the speaker's pronunciation. To suggest otherwise is to confuse unfamiliarity with inferiority. I would not wish to be unfair: many employers act in good faith, and some have introduced training to counter unconscious bias. Nevertheless, good intentions do not amount to good practice, and I would respectfully suggest that firms review how interviews are scored and whether accent has any bearing on the outcome.

I would therefore urge your readers, and indeed your editorial team, not to postpone this conversation any further. Should you consider the matter worthy of a follow-up, I would be happy to share the evidence on which this letter is based.

Yours faithfully,

Elena Marsh

P.S. to Sam: Just sent a letter to the paper about accent bias at work, so fingers crossed they'll print it! Can't believe nobody's covered it properly before. Let's catch up soon, yeah?

reading.title: The Accent Question
reading.intro: Read the article and answer the questions. Pay attention to inferences, not only to explicit facts.
paragraphs: When Marisol Vega moved from Monterrey to Manchester at the age of twenty-six, she assumed that her English, honed over a decade of careful study, would see her through. It did, more or less. What she had not anticipated was the way people would listen to her. Within a fortnight a colleague had remarked, with every appearance of kindness, that she was 'remarkably easy to understand, considering'. The 'considering' stayed with her for months.

Linguists have a name for what Marisol was experiencing: accentism, or linguistic prejudice. Every speaker has an accent; there is no such thing as speaking 'without one'. Yet certain accents, historically those associated with power, education and the capital, have come to be treated as neutral, while others are heard as markers of something to be explained or excused. In Britain, Received Pronunciation, spoken natively by only a small fraction of the population, long served as the voice of the BBC and of the boardroom. Regional voices, from the Glasgow patter to the Liverpool lilt, were politely tolerated at best and, at worst, treated as a sign of limited ability. That hierarchy has loosened, but it has not vanished.

Marisol's first response was to try to iron out her accent. She watched dozens of hours of television, recorded herself reading the news aloud, and picked up the flat vowels of her adopted city with surprising speed. Colleagues noticed. 'You sound so Mancunian,' one said, and it was impossible to tell whether it was praise. Meanwhile, something odd was happening at the other end of the line. When she phoned her mother, her Spanish had begun to come across as slightly stiff, as though it, too, were being performed. Her sister teased her for sprinkling English words into their conversations: 'Estoy un poco stressed', 'nos vemos el weekend'. Marisol laughed it off, but privately she wondered whether she was losing something.

What she was actually doing, as the sociolinguist she eventually consulted explained, was code-switching: the fluid movement between languages or registers depending on who is listening and what is at stake. Far from being a sign of confusion, it is a sophisticated skill, one that bilinguals deploy almost instinctively. People code-switch not only between languages but within one. The same person may speak very differently to a child, a client and a childhood friend, and nobody calls that dishonest. 'The danger,' the linguist said, 'is not in adapting. It is in believing that one version of you is the real one and the rest are costumes.'

That remark changed the way Marisol thought about her situation. Identity, she began to see, is not a fixed possession, like a passport, but something negotiated in conversation, again and again. Her heritage was not diminished by her new vowels, any more than a Mancunian's roots are erased by a spell in Madrid. What mattered was whether she retained a sense of choice. Some days she wished to blend in; on others she wanted to stand out; and the freedom to decide, she realised, was precisely what linguistic prejudice takes away.

Today Marisol teaches Spanish at a community college, and she begins every first lesson in the same way. She asks her students to introduce themselves, then points out that nobody in the room has a 'neutral' voice. Those who worry about their accents are told, firmly but kindly, that intelligibility matters, while sounding like someone else does not. She still gets the occasional compliment on her English, and she has stopped trying to decide whether each one is a kindness or a verdict, because she has learned that the answer matters far less than her own freedom to answer in whichever voice she chooses. These days she thanks the speaker without a flicker of resentment and says, with a smile that is only slightly mischievous, 'Considering what?'

listening.title: Between two voices
listening.intro: Listen to an excerpt from a radio programme about accents and register. You can repeat it.

lines.text: Welcome back to Word of Mouth. Today we're asking why we sound different depending on who we're talking to. With me is Dr Amara Okafor, a sociolinguist. Amara, welcome.
Thanks for having me. It's a subject close to my heart, because I do it all the time myself.
Switch. When I'm lecturing, I sound fairly formal. But at my mum's in Leeds, I slip into the dialect I grew up with, and my vowels change completely. My students wouldn't recognise me.
And that's not, you know, putting on a voice?
Not at all. It's closer to dressing for the weather. Nobody thinks you've lost your identity because you've swapped a suit for a raincoat.
We've got a caller on the line. Daniel, you're through.

Hi there. I just wanted to say that at work I'm constantly toning my accent down. I'm from Glasgow, and I was told in a meeting that I should 'speak more clearly'. I speak perfectly clearly. I just don't sound like them.
That's a very common experience, Daniel. We call it accent prejudice, and the research suggests that listeners often judge competence by sound rather than substance. It's a bias, not a fact.
But surely there's a case for a standard? A shared form we can all understand?
There is, for writing and for certain official purposes. But being understood and sounding the same are not the same thing. I can follow Daniel perfectly, and I'd bet most of your listeners can too.
Cheers. That's a relief to hear. I'd started to think I was the one at fault.
Well, I think that's a good place to leave it. Amara, thank you. And Daniel, don't let anyone water down your voice.
Hear, hear. Thanks for having me.

tasks.prompt: Talk about how your way of speaking changes depending on who you are with: family, work, friends. Describe one specific case of code-switching.

tasks.model: I'm a bit of a chameleon, to be honest. At work I tone down my slang and sound quite measured, but with my cousins I slip into a much looser, jokier way of talking. Without noticing it, I pick up their expressions, and then they rub off on my colleagues! My grandmother has a way with words that simply gets lost in translation. I wouldn't say I'm putting on a voice. It's more that I'm dressing for the weather.
checklist: A clear register contrast between two contexts
At least 3 phrasal verbs (slip into, tone down, rub off on, pick up)
One idiom about language, used naturally
Cohesion: to be honest, more that…

tasks.prompt: Give an explanation in two registers: first formally tell a client that a shipment will be delayed; then tell a close colleague.
questions: How would you explain the delay to a client you have never met?
How would you say the same thing to a close colleague?

tasks.model: To the client: I should like to inform you that, regrettably, your order will be delayed until Thursday. Please accept my apologies for any inconvenience. To a colleague: Heads up, the order's running late, probably Thursday. Sorry about that. The shift is mainly lexical, with 'regrettably' and 'inconvenience' replaced by 'heads up' and 'running late'. With the client, a euphemism like 'a slight delay' keeps the tone calm.
checklist: Two versions with clearly different registers
Formal formulas (I should like to inform you…, Please accept my apologies)
Colloquial vocabulary in the second version (heads up, running late)
Comment on what changes between the two

tasks.prompt: Discussion: "Accents should be neutralised for professional communication." Defend or reject the claim with arguments and an example.
questions: Do you agree that accents should be neutralised at work?
Where is the line between clarity and conformity?
What happens to a language when its dialects die out?
tasks.model: I'd push back on that. Being understood matters, but sounding the same doesn't. A 'neutral' accent is really just the voice of whoever holds power, and asking people to tone theirs down makes them feel like outsiders. If dialects die out, we lose more than sounds: we lose a way of seeing the world. That said, I'll grant you that in an emergency call, clarity is vital.
checklist: A clear position from the first sentence
Distinguish clarity from uniformity
One phrasal verb (die out, tone down) and identity vocabulary
A final concession with nuance (I'll grant you…)
